solutions.latex: Let $\alpha$ be the angle the line makes with the positive $x$-axis: $\tan\alpha=-\sqrt{3}$, so $\alpha=120^\circ$. Then $\theta=180^\circ-\alpha=60^\circ$. Answer B.
At $A$ the curve is increasing, so $f'(x)>0$; it is concave up, so $f''(x)>0$. Answer C.
$\dot{x}<0$ so the particle moves left; $\ddot{x}<0$ so its speed increases to the left. Answer C.
Third angle: $180^\circ-(42^\circ+67^\circ)=71^\circ$. Sine rule: $\dfrac{x}{\sin 67^\circ}=\dfrac{y}{\sin 71^\circ}$, so $x=\dfrac{y\sin 67^\circ}{\sin 71^\circ}$. Answer A.
Centre $y=-2$, amplitude $4$, so range is $[-2-4,\,-2+4]=[-6,2]$. Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. Answer D.
The particle is at the origin when the (signed) area under the velocity-time graph is $0$, which occurs at $t=4$. Answer C.
$f(-x)=3+2x$ and $h(x)=\ln(3+2x)$ is only defined for $3+2x>0$, so $x>-\dfrac{3}{2}$. Answer B.

solutions.question: 11(c)
solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-3$. When $x=2$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2(2)-3=1$.

So $m=1$ at $(2,-7)$ and the tangent is $y-(-7)=1(x-2)$, i.e. $y+7=x-2$, giving $x-y-9=0$.

solutions.question: 11(f)
solutions.latex:
Quotient rule with $u=x^{4}$, $v=\cos x$, $u'=4x^{3}$, $v'=-\sin x$:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\cos x\cdot 4x^{3}-x^{4}(-\sin x)}{\cos^{2}x}=\dfrac{x^{3}\left(4\cos x+x\sin x\right)}{\cos^{2}x}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct $u'$ and $v'$ / quotient rule set up; 1: correct simplified derivative

solutions.question: 12(c)
solutions.latex:
$\angle RPQ=90^\circ-70^\circ=20^\circ$. Cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$:

$RQ^{2}=16^{2}+35^{2}-2\times16\times35\times\cos 20^\circ=428.54\ldots$

solutions.question: 12(c)
solutions.latex:
Let $\angle RQP=\theta$. Sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{16}=\dfrac{\sin 20^\circ}{20.7}$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{16\sin 20^\circ}{20.7}$ and $\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.264)=15.3^\circ$.

Since the angle sum of $\triangle PQR$ would exceed $180^\circ$ if $\theta=180^\circ-15.3^\circ=164.7^\circ$, $\theta$ is acute.

Or by the cosine rule: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{20.7^{2}+35^{2}-16^{2}}{2\times20.7\times35}=0.9645$, so $\theta=15.30^\circ$.

Bearing $=270^\circ+15^\circ=285^\circ$ (nearest degree).
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct use of sine or cosine rule for $\theta$; 1: bearing $285^\circ$

solutions.question: 14(d)
solutions.latex:
$\tan^{2}x-1=0$ or $\sin^{2}x-3\cos^{2}x=0$.

$\tan x=\pm1$, acute related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

$\sin^{2}x=3\cos^{2}x$, $\tan^{2}x=3$ (note $\cos^{2}x=0$ is not a solution), $\tan x=\pm\sqrt{3}$, acute related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Alternatively, $\sin^{2}x-3(1-\sin^{2}x)=0$, $4\sin^{2}x=3$, $\sin x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, giving the same solutions.

Solutions: $x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4},\pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3},\pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: separating into two factors; 1: solutions from $\tan^2x=1$; 1: solutions from the second factor

solutions.question: 15(b)
solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=32\times2\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{90}\right)=-\dfrac{64}{90}\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)$

When $t=45$: $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-\dfrac{64}{90}\left(1-\dfrac{45}{90}\right)=-\dfrac{64}{90}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=-\dfrac{32}{90}=-\dfrac{16}{45}$

The water is draining at $\dfrac{16}{45}$ litres/sec when the cooler is one-quarter full.

solutions.question: 16(b)
solutions.latex:
By Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle FOB$: $x^{2}+y^{2}=\left(\sqrt{5}\right)^{2}$, so $y=\sqrt{5-x^{2}}$.

$L=AB+DC+FG=2x+2x+2y=4x+2\sqrt{5-x^{2}}$

solutions.question: 16(b)
solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{dL}{dx}=4+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(5-x^{2}\right)^{-1/2}\times(-2x)=4-\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{5-x^{2}}}$

For a maximum/minimum $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$: $\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{5-x^{2}}}=4$, $2x=4\sqrt{5-x^{2}}$.

Squaring: $4x^{2}=16(5-x^{2})$, $x^{2}=4(5-x^{2})=20-4x^{2}$, $5x^{2}=20$, $x^{2}=4$, $x=\pm2$.

Since $x$ is a length, consider $x=2$:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x&1&2&2.1\\\hline \dfrac{dL}{dx}&3&0&-1.47\end{array}$$

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so there is a relative maximum at $x=2$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: derivative; 1: $x=2$; 1: check that it is a maximum

solutions.question: 16(c)
solutions.latex:
$A_{2}=135\,000\beta^{2}-M\beta-M$

So $A_{n}=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\beta^{n-1}-M\beta^{n-2}-\cdots-M=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\left(1+\beta+\beta^{2}+\cdots+\beta^{n-1}\right)$

The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=\beta$ and $n$ terms:

$A_{n}=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\dfrac{1\left(\beta^{n}-1\right)}{\beta-1}=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\dfrac{\beta^{n}-1}{\frac{0.05}{k}}=135\,000\beta^{n}-\dfrac{kM\left(\beta^{n}-1\right)}{0.05}$ as required.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: expressing $A_n$ with the geometric series; 1: summing the series and substituting $\beta-1=\frac{0.05}{k}$
